sections.heading: Translation of the Relic of Venerable Maximus the Confessor

pairs.en: On the same day, the thirteenth of the month, the bringing-back and transfer of the relic of our venerable father MAXIMUS the Confessor.
*The faithful move your dust, Maximus, showing* *that you are alive, by changing even its resting-place.* *Maximus' body, dead, they transferred around the thirteenth.*

For the Synaxarion of Saint Maximus, see the twenty-first of January, when his memory is kept. See also his full life in the New Paradise; his Greek life survives in the Holy Monastery of Iveron, and elsewhere, and it begins: “When Herakleios held the sceptres of rule.”
On the same day, Saint EUDOCIA the empress died in peace.
*Now, Saviour, more fittingly than before, standing* *before your Father, you say: my good pleasure, Father.*

This Eudocia was the daughter of Leontios, an Athenian sophist, and her father taught her, with distinction, every kind of learning. The emperor Theodosios the Younger took her as his wife, through the good offices of his sister Pulcheria. She had previously been called Athenaïs; she was baptised by Attikos, the Patriarch of Constantinople, and renamed Eudocia, to Theodosios' delight. She also wrote a heroic poem about the Persian war, according to Sokrates the church historian.

To her are also ascribed the Homeric centos on Christ — poems stitched together out of lines of Homer — as many hold; others ascribe them to the empress Eudocia, the wife of the emperor Constantine Doukas, who reigned in the year 1060. So much for what Meletios says. The blessed Dositheos says that when the venerable Melania the Younger came to Constantinople, she spoke at length to Eudocia to move her to compassion for the holy places of Jerusalem. Eudocia therefore grew to love her, and kept her as a comfort. Moved by this, Eudocia went to Jerusalem, where the venerable sites of pilgrimage are, as Sokrates recounts in the seventh book of his History, and she stayed there for a year, as Evagrios says, and founded a lavra — a large community of monks — and women's monasteries. She also renewed the walls of Jerusalem, so that on her account the prophecy of king David was fulfilled, which says: “Do good, O Lord, in your good pleasure to Sion, and the walls of Jerusalem shall be built.” She built, too, a church of the Protomartyr Stephen, one stadion away from Jerusalem. All this Eudocia did after the death of Theodosios, when Markianos reigned; for it was then that she returned to Jerusalem, and she stayed there until the end of her life, as Evagrios records in the first book of his History.

She too was once deceived by the Monophysite Theodosios, and fell into the heresy of the Monophysites — those who confess only one nature in Christ. But when she learned that her son-in-law Olybrios had been murdered, and that his children and her daughter Plakidia had been carried off as captives to Karthagene by Gizeric, she said in prayer that word of David, “Your chastening itself shall teach me” — that is, “it will bring me to my senses.” And so she sent to Symeon the Stylite, the saint who lived on top of a pillar, asking what the Orthodox belief is. He sent word back to her: you have the great Euthymios there — why ask me? So Euthymios catechised her and set her right, as Kyrillos, the disciple of Euthymios, attests.

sections.heading: Venerable Seridos, Abbot of the Gaza Monastery

pairs.en: The venerable SERIDOS, abbot of the monastery at Gaza, died in peace.
*Where you are, there is Seridos too, O Word of God,* *gazing on the glory the Father has given you.*

This venerable Seridos was abbot of that great community near Gaza, where Saint Barsanouphios and his disciple John lived, and Abba Dorotheos. See about him in the Catecheses of Abba Dorotheos, and in the Book of Saint Barsanouphios.

Our venerable and God-bearing father DOROTHEOS, who first lived the ascetic life in the community of Abba Seridos near Gaza, and later founded a monastery of his own, after the death of Abba John called the Prophet, and after the great Barsanouphios had withdrawn into complete silence, died in peace.
*Discernment flowed into your words,* *Dorotheos, the glory of monks.*

How great a discernment this venerable Dorotheos reached through his obedience and humility is attested by his own discourses, found in the volume that contains the Catecheses of Theodore the Studite. Other writings of the same Dorotheos are also found in manuscripts.
The venerable DOSITHEOS the disciple, who lived the ascetic life in Abba Seridos' community under the care of Saint Dorotheos, died in peace.
*You were shown to be obedience traced in lines,* *Dositheos, the bright ornament of all who serve.*

About this venerable Dositheos, see the first discourse of Abba Dorotheos in the Catecheses of the Studite — Dorotheos, who was both his elder and his superior — to learn how this blessed man stood as the very image of obedience and submission, the living example that all disciples and subordinates ought to have, so that they too may be counted worthy of the same glory as his in the kingdom of the heavens.

We remember the renowned and all-blessed empress IRENE, foundress of the revered monastery of Christ the Saviour Pantokrator — the Almighty — who was renamed Xene, “the stranger,” when she took the holy and angelic habit of the nuns.
*The Almighty has given you a dwelling above,* *as foundress of your own dwelling below.*

It was fitting that Constantinople, that greatest of cities, set above all others, should not adorn herself only with the beauty of buildings that decay, nor take her joy in the tales of the men of old, renowned as they were for their virtues; but rather that she should boast and take pride in the renowned empress Irene, the foundress of the monastery of the Pantokrator. For one thing, once the old stories about her had faded with the passing of so much time, the gladness and joy that came from them had become useless to lovers of beauty. But the beauty and splendour born of the monastery of the Pantokrator, which this renowned empress Irene built from its very foundations, shines with its rays over all the beauties of the city that time had quenched. And for another thing, this empress Irene had gathered every virtue into herself from childhood, and having become a vessel of all that is good, she stood as an adornment also for the God-crowned and purple-born emperor, her husband.

This renowned empress was born to fortunate parents, kings of the West. And from her early youth the blessed one showed what she would become later, just as noble trees show from their first budding what fruits they are going to bear. So as she grew and advanced, she became famous and renowned to everyone — for virtue has a way of making known those who practise it, even when they are still hidden in some corner or out-of-the-way place. And since at that time the renowned emperors — Alexios Komnenos, I mean, and his wife Irene, who reigned in the year 1070 — were looking for a beautiful and virtuous maiden, they found this renowned Irene, who had every good thing in herself, and they joined her in marriage to their God-given offspring, the purple-born emperor John. Then everything was filled with joy and gladness. (The book's own footnote here reads: “In the year 1081 Alexios Komnenos succeeded Botaneiates.”)

So the blessed one bore the said John eight children, four boys and four girls, whom she raised magnificently and royally. Later, reckoning that the cheerful things of this world, and even the empire itself, are nothing, she would say quietly to herself that word of David: “What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to the pit?” So night and day the thrice-blessed one never stopped serving God with the intercessions and appeals she made to the emperor for the help of those in need, protecting and in every way doing good to those who lacked anything, and taking more joy in giving and showing mercy to the poor than in receiving from others. And whatever money came into her hands before she was crowned empress, she shared it all out among the poor. She was the protector of orphans and widows; she enriched the monasteries with funds. As for her other virtues, how can I recount them? How can I show her gentleness? Her stillness? Her humility? Her compassion for everyone? Her graciousness? The sweetness of her speech? Her freedom from anger? For the blessed one was never angry, nor moved to insult or revenge anyone; and if she ever had occasion to smile, even her smile was modest and restrained. She was always in mourning, always grieving over herself — and so the penitential psalms of David were always on her lips. And since she prided herself on self-control, she loved to dry out her body with plain, unseasoned food, choosing to live ascetically. Yet the praiseworthy one did not reckon all this enough to please her God-loving purpose; so when she later became empress, she despised all the things of empire, and even the very necessities of life.

For this reason the renowned one built, from the very foundations, the imperial monastery named after the Pantokrator, together with the beautiful churches, hospices, and old-age homes that are still to be seen — which surpassed the ancient churches, hospices, and old-age homes, old and new alike, in situation and in beauty. Helping greatly with the building and the fine proportions of all these edifices was a new Bezalel — the much-honoured Nikephoros, I mean, the most trusted man of this blessed Irene — who with such great zeal and eagerness saw to the completion of these sacred buildings that the renowned man gave no sleep to his eyes nor rest to his temples. So when the renowned Irene had completed all these works with the help of the said Nikephoros, she brought to Constantinople, the queen of cities, a delightful and gladdening ornament, rejoicing in their success and beauty, and thanking God for them. (The book's own footnote here sends the reader to 26 October, to the footnote on the translation of the icon of Saint Demetrios from Thessaloniki to the Queen City, for more about this most beautiful and renowned monastery of the Pantokrator.)

And since the blessed one needed a yet greater helper to accomplish her God-pleasing purposes, she found one. One day she took her husband the emperor by the hand and led him into the beautiful church of the Pantokrator which she had built. Then she fell to the ground, pressed her head against the holy floor of the church, and said with tears: “Accept, O Master — accept, for your own grace's sake, the church built by God.” Adding tears to tears, the blessed one declared that she would not rise from the floor until she had full assurance of her request. And when she heard the emperor promise that he would fulfil her request and her desire — that he would strive even beyond his power to dedicate sacred treasures and various properties to the church; that through movable and immovable goods and annual revenues he would establish this revered monastery to hold the first place and rank among all the monasteries of the city; and that our Lord Jesus Christ, worshipped and honoured in it, would henceforth be called Pantokrator there, as he truly is and is called — when the renowned Irene heard these words, she rose from the ground full of unspeakable joy. And from then on she rejoiced in the spirit, since she had cast from her mind the weight and the care of the monastery. Not much time passed, and the renowned one went to Bithynia, and there she departed to the Lord Pantokrator whom she had longed for. Her precious relic was laid to rest in the monastery of the Pantokrator that she herself had built. And when the promise that the pious emperor had made was fulfilled, then the monastery of the Pantokrator grew and was enlarged so much that it held the first place among all the monasteries of Constantinople. A little later, the most pious and renowned emperor John himself also left this earthly empire, and passed over to the heavenly Master and king, God. His relic too was laid to rest in the same monastery of the Pantokrator, which he had enlarged and made splendid.
The holy martyr CORONATOS died by the sword.
*Offering his neck to the blade, Coronatos* *slays the many-necked hydra, error.*
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
